points: Metals (aluminium and tin) are strong and airtight; they are used for canned fish and fruit, takeaway containers and aerosol whipped cream. Tins are lacquered inside so the metal does not react with the food.
Glass (jars and bottles) is hygienic, transparent and reusable; it is used for beverages, mayonnaise, sauces, preserves and cooking oil.
Plastics (polythene, PET and similar polymers) are lightweight, flexible and moisture-proof; they are used for polythene bags, PET soft drink bottles, yoghurt pots, dairy spreads and dried pasta.
Polystyrene is lightweight, insulating, shock-absorbing and easily moulded; it is used for egg trays and takeaway trays, and is not readily biodegradable.
Paper and cardboard are light, inexpensive, easy to print on and renewable; they are used for cereal boxes, egg cartons and paper bags for bread, cakes, flour and sugar.
Waxed cartons use a wax coating to make the board waterproof; they are cheap, lightweight, printable and heat-sealable.
Packaging must be strong and durable enough to survive handling and transport.
It must be airtight or moisture- and vapour-proof, depending on the food.
It must be hygienic and safe, and must not react with or taint the food, so it should be odourless.
It should be easy to open and, where needed, easy to reseal.
It should be lightweight, stackable and easy to store.
It should be heat resistant where the food is heated in the pack, and printable so that labels can be applied.
It should be attractive to the consumer and economical to produce.
Protection: packaging guards food against physical damage and against contamination by micro-organisms and dirt.
Containment: it holds the product in the portion size intended for the consumer.
Information: it carries the product name, ingredients, nutrition and storage details.
Tamper evidence: a sealed pack shows whether the contents have been interfered with.
Metal and plastic packaging is not biodegradable and is made from non-renewable resources, but both can be recycled.
Glass can be reused and recycled indefinitely without losing quality.
Paper and cardboard are made from a renewable resource, are biodegradable and are widely recyclable.
Polystyrene is bulky and not readily biodegradable, so its environmental impact depends on whether it is collected for recycling.
The impact is reduced by using less packaging, reusing containers and recycling materials.
Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP): the air is removed and replaced with a controlled mixture of carbon dioxide, nitrogen and oxygen, and the pack is heat sealed.
The gas mixture slows the growth of bacteria, yeasts and moulds, so the shelf life of the food is extended.
MAP is used for fresh meat, fish, fruit and vegetables, baked goods and cheese.
Biodegradable packaging breaks down into the raw materials of nature, with micro-organisms doing much of the work.
Examples of biodegradable packaging: paper bags for bread, cakes, sugar and flour, and cardboard for cereals, takeaway foods and eggs.
Diagram: a labelled sealed pack showing the gas mixture inside the tray and the heat-sealed film lid.

notes.b: The European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014 give effect in Ireland to Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, and the Food Safety Authority of Ireland enforces them.
points: The name of the food must be stated, along with a list of ingredients in descending order by weight.
Allergens such as milk, egg, nuts and gluten cereals must be emphasised within the ingredients list.
The net quantity must be stated, and the name and address of the food business operator must appear on the label.
A use-by date is given for highly perishable food and is a food safety date; a best-before date is a quality date, after which the food may still be safe.
Storage conditions and cooking or usage instructions must be given, for example keep refrigerated or stir before use.
A lot or batch code is shown for traceability, and the country of origin is given where the law requires it.
Additives are identified by their class name followed by the specific name or E number.
The mandatory nutrition declaration gives energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt.
Values are given per 100 g or 100 ml, and often per portion as well.
Claims such as low fat or contains live cultures must be accurate and not misleading, and nutrition and health claims must meet the EU rules.
Low fat does not necessarily mean low sugar, salt or energy, so the full declaration must be read.

notes.h: Labelling as a source of consumer information
points: Labels allow consumers to compare products on energy, fat, sugar and salt, rather than being guided by brand, pictures or health claims.
Consumers following a low-salt, low-saturated-fat or high-fibre diet can select products by their declared values.
Ingredients and allergen emphasis protect people with coeliac disease, milk, egg, nut or other allergies.
Use-by and best-before dates, storage and reheating instructions protect safety and reduce food waste.
The manufacturer's details and the lot code support traceability and complaints.
Quality assurance, organic, fair-trade and gluten-free marks guide consumers with particular ethical or dietary choices.

keyTerms.definition: Packaging in which the air is replaced with a controlled mixture of gases, then heat sealed, to slow the spoilage of food.
Packaging that breaks down into the raw materials of nature through the action of micro-organisms.
Describes a material that can be collected and reprocessed into new products.
A coating applied inside metal cans so that the metal does not react with the food.
A sealed pack design that shows clearly whether the contents have been opened or interfered with.
A date after which a highly perishable food should not be eaten, for safety reasons.
A date after which a food may lose quality, though it is not necessarily unsafe.
Showing an allergenic ingredient in the ingredients list in a way that makes it stand out, such as bold type.
The standard panel of energy and nutrient values that manufacturers must give on the label of most pre-packed foods.
A batch code printed on packaging that allows a product to be traced back through production and distribution.

factCards.term: Five desirable characteristics of food packaging
factCards.definition: Strong and durable; airtight or moisture-proof; hygienic and safe; easy to open and reseal; lightweight and easy to store.

factCards.term: Three advantages of paper and cardboard packaging
factCards.definition: They are light and relatively inexpensive, easy to print on for labelling, and made from a renewable resource that is biodegradable and recyclable.

factCards.term: Gases used in modified atmosphere packaging
factCards.definition: Carbon dioxide, nitrogen and oxygen, in a controlled mixture.

factCards.term: Why nitrogen is used in food packs
factCards.definition: It is inert, so it displaces oxygen and prevents oxidation and spoilage.

factCards.term: Items in the mandatory nutrition declaration
factCards.definition: Energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt.

factCards.term: Difference between use-by and best-before dates
factCards.definition: A use-by date is a food safety date for highly perishable food; a best-before date is a quality date.
Comparing products, selecting diets, protecting people with allergies, and reducing waste through correct storage and use.

factCards.term: Purpose of lacquer in a tin can
factCards.definition: It stops the metal reacting with the food.

questions.prompt: Explain why glass and paper are used to package different types of food. Give one example of each material and a reason it suits the food it holds.
questions.model: Glass is used for beverages, sauces, preserves and oil. It is transparent so the product can be seen, it is inert so it does not react with the food, and it is hygienic and reusable or recyclable. Paper and cardboard are used for cereals, eggs, bread and cakes. They are light, cheap, easy to print on for labelling and protective enough for dry or fragile foods, and they are biodegradable and recyclable. Full marks need one example and one reason for each material.

questions.prompt: Assess how the packaging and labelling of a food product serve the manufacturer, the consumer and the environment, and identify one limitation of each.
questions.model: Manufacturer: packaging protects the product, extends its shelf life through methods such as modified atmosphere packaging, carries branding and gives a tamper-evident seal; the label meets legal requirements and identifies the batch for traceability. Limitation: packaging adds cost and must meet the labelling rules, which can be time-consuming. Consumer: the label gives the ingredients in order of weight, allergens emphasised, the nutrition declaration per 100 g and per portion, use-by or best-before dates and storage instructions, so choices and safety are informed. Limitation: a label can be misread, as low fat does not mean low sugar, salt or energy. Environment: material choice matters; glass is reusable and recyclable, paper and cardboard are renewable and biodegradable, and metal and plastic are recyclable but not biodegradable. Limitation: excess packaging creates waste, so reducing and reusing it is the best response.
